Infinity exists as a totally useful and usable, and not to mention important, mathematical concept, even if we can't count to it or enumerate a set that is explicitly infinte. And while we can't necessarily generate random numbers from a pathological distribution with undefined moments (e.g. no mean or variance) directly, we can transform the random numbers we can generate (i.e. the uniform random numbers between 0 and 1) into those sorts of distributions in much the same way as we can map a circle to the real number line.

You seem to be implying "deterministic" means "predictable" in the broad sense of knowing the distribution of a phenomena. By that definition, pathological things like Pareto distributions are "deterministic," since we know that a certain percentage of samples will be within certain bounds (e.g. the 80:20 rule).

Certainly, any set of numbers we can generate or data we can collect will necessarily be finite, and as such we will only be able to ultimately guess at the true distribution. However that does not mean we must suffer in ignorance. We can construct statistics that estimate parameters that do define these distributions from known data. And we know the distribution of those parameters are not pathological and can be determined with reasonable accuracy.

More technical discussion can be found in references about pathological statistical distributions and likelihood estimation. Nontechnical discussion can be found in references about Black Swan events.
